summary: RP1 Spatial Fabric is the idea that a place in three dimensions can be a document with a URL, the way a web page is, plus the stack that makes that real: a signed fabric file, a native engine that reads it, and a browser that opens it. The fabric file is a compact JSON Web Signature over a JSON manifest, signed RS256 against an X.509 chain carried in the header, listing WebAssembly modules that may be pinned by hash and a scene tree of packed 528-byte node records with 64-bit positions; a portal is simply a node with subtype 255 whose resource reference is the URL of another fabric, so fabrics nest and each nested one is verified on its own. Correction, dated 2026-09-03: this record previously said the browser had no public source and that two engine dependencies were private, which was true when it was observed on 2026-08-13 and is not true now; since 2026-09-01 the engine Sneeze, the browser Rubidium, the realtime library RMAP, the map library Map and the guest SDK are all public repositories, and the engine's dependency manifest clones the two former blockers from public addresses. Read the licences before reusing any of it: the engine, the SDK and RMAP are Apache-2.0, the browser's own README calls it proprietary with all rights reserved, and Map ships no licence file. The trap is smaller than it was but still the main one: there is now a published interface header the vendor calls the canonical frozen contract, but there is still no fabric-file specification and no conformance suite, so compatible with this format has no testable meaning, and three incompatible manifest dialects still ship together inside one public repository at one commit, including a signed sample whose payload disagrees with the unsigned source file beside it. Signing works and is stable, but signature acceptance is not scene compatibility, and the vendor's own documentation records that the browser currently pins the trust level instead of acting on the one it computed.

coverage.note: The fabric file is the container: a compact JSON Web Signature whose payload holds the serialized manifest under a data claim, with members for container name, declared services and a module list of url and hash pairs, and the scene tree under Data.Scene. The public sample fabric in the engine repository is exactly that, and the browser signs and verifies these files from its own command line.

coverage.note: Position, rotation and scale are three, four and three 64-bit floats at fixed offsets in a 528-byte record, and every node composes a full translate-rotate-scale and inherits its parent's, with no class exception. That precision is unusually good. But no handedness and no up axis is declared anywhere in the wire record or the published interface header: the shipped corpus is Z-up purely by convention. The local row records an observed integration failure that no public file states: mounting one of these fabrics into a Y-up host laid the scene on its side with no error, so the integration had to make an up-axis declaration required with no default.

coverage.note: The wire record declares no units. The engine has since dropped its astronomical-unit path and accumulates all geometry in metres, which removes one trap, but it still gives each scene one flattening factor computed from that scene's own reach, so authored size is not what reaches the screen and a nested child inherits the parent's factor rather than getting its own. The only way to gain precision inside a body is to make that fabric the root. The local row records an observed composition failure that no public file states: a fabric whose native unit was the astronomical unit read as one metre when composed into a one-to-one room, so the integration had to make a units-per-metre value required with no default.

coverage.note: The signature answers who published these bytes: RS256 over an X.509 chain carried in the JWS header, and the publisher's durable identity is the SHA-256 of the leaf certificate's public key, so it survives certificate renewal. Two cautions, both from the vendor's own public material. The sample fabric shipped in the engine repository is signed by a test certificate authority, not public infrastructure. And the browser does not yet act on the trust it computes: the documentation says the container-open path pins the level instead. The local row records a fact no public file states: a browser-based reader cannot build an X.509 path or read the operating system trust store, so a web reader can only make a labelled claim.

coverage.note: Modules may be pinned by an exact SHA-256 in the manifest, in the subresource-integrity spelling, and the fetch layer refuses a body whose digest does not match. The hole is structural and is provable from the public source: the manifest reader takes the hash only if the key is present, the verifier returns success when the hash string is empty, and public sample fabrics in both the engine repository and the tutorial documentation ship modules with no hash at all. A validly signed manifest may therefore cover the manifest but not the module bytes.

coverage.note: Nested fabrics compose recursively. A node marked as an attachment point starts a fetch of the child fabric, and the parent's scene code parses that child and verifies its signature and chain on its own, so a trusted parent confers nothing on an unverified child. The composition is transclusion, not travel: the child is drawn in the parent's accumulated frame. The local row records an observed property no public file states: cycles and fan-out were proven bounded in this project's working reader.

coverage.note: Real isolation exists and is documented: each module instance gets its own linear memory, and console, storage and network handles are scoped to the publisher's identity so one source cannot read another's cached files, stored documents or log stream. What is missing is the permission half. There is no grant, scope or capability of any kind in the interface registry, and the vendor's own documentation says the access-control checks are defined but the host functions do not yet consistently call them. The ownership functions are present in the engine source and no caller anywhere in the tree calls them. A signature says who wrote the code and has never said what the code may do.

coverage.note: This has changed since the earlier reading and the change is real. The published interface now carries a wall clock and a monotonic clock as first-class subsystems, with a defined base of one sixty-fourth of a second since 1601 in universal time, and a timer service that actually fires: a metronome wakes a timer pool about a thousand times a second and delivers the event back into the guest. What is still absent is the shared part of the capability. Nothing agrees a clock between two publishers or across a network, and the orbit period and origin fields in the wire record still carry no declared unit or zero point, so astronomical time cannot be reproduced from the file alone.

coverage.note: The format encodes no meshes itself. A node names an external resource by reference and the engine decides what it is by content, parsing a binary or JSON glTF into a render model and treating anything else as an image texture; the tutorial fabrics resolve those references to glTF binary files. Geometry is therefore delegated to a registered format and only the reference is standardised. Two of the vendor's own public notes disagree about what is then drawn: the scene note says the built model is read from the node, while the compositor note says glTF binaries are not parsed there and physical nodes render as boxes for now.

coverage.note: Lighting is now documented in public. Scene-wide ambient and directional light are authored in the manifest's Primary block and are scene properties, not nodes, so a local object cannot alter global illumination; placed point and spot lights are ordinary nodes carrying colour, intensity and cone angles. The composition rule the integration once had to derive from source is now stated: a placed light's intensity is multiplied by the square of its world scale times the scene's flattening scale. There is no indirect light, no shadow model and no probe model anywhere in the format.

coverage.note: The interface half of this is fixed and the file half is not. The published interface header now carries a version constant that moves only for a framing change, and method numbers are permanent and append-only, so an old module keeps loading. The fabric file has no format-version field and the dialects still disagree inside one public repository at one commit: one sample manifest uses lower-case keys with url and hash, its neighbour uses capitalised keys with sUrl and sHash, and the signed sample's own payload uses the lower-case spelling while the unsigned source beside it uses the capitalised one. The services block is described three different ways in public: a name-keyed object in the engine note, an array in every sample, and a list of name, type, endpoint and modules records in the documentation. The vendor states outright that the format is not stable before version 1.0.0 and that fabrics made before this release must be updated. The local row records an observed link mismatch from the 2026-07 to 2026-08 generation that no public source states, and the single-Call interface has since removed that failure mode.

coverage.note: The browser architecture names scene understanding among the capabilities it expects, and hands every one of them to OpenXR extensions rather than defining anything itself. So a reconstruction of the room may reach an application through the runtime underneath, but this project's own specification carries no room geometry, no format for it and no way to pass it on.

sources.title: Sneeze architecture, the project's own standards proposal for the metaverse browser engine
sources.quote: Hand tracking, eye tracking, face tracking, passthrough (AR/MR), scene understanding, spatial anchors. These capabilities are provided through OpenXR extensions without breaking the core specification.

coverage.note: Semantic labelling of real surfaces is inside the same deferral: it belongs to the scene understanding the architecture leaves to OpenXR. Nothing in the project's own interfaces names a real floor, wall or object.

coverage.note: No depth of the real world is defined. The architecture treats the raw camera feed of the user's surroundings as data of extreme sensitivity to be kept away from content, and defines no depth channel of its own.

coverage.note: RP1's published work is the spatial fabric format and the server that serves it. The client decides what to do with a camera view of the room and nothing in the fabric addresses it.
The fabric carries scene nodes and modules. There is no input model in it that would deliver a live reading of the user's face or body to a running module.

A fabric is a signed tree of nodes with attachment points and modules, and it is opened by a client that then has to work out the floor for itself. Nothing in the format declares walkable surface, bounds or a spawn point, so two clients opening the same fabric may put a person in different places.

coverage.note: A fabric is signed and its signature chain is verified before it is parsed, which answers who sent it, not what review it has had. There is no field for a review record and no service in the path that performs one, so a receiving client learns nothing about whether anybody looked at the content.

coverage.note: The fabric has no geographic frame; the project's own material records earth-scale coordinate ownership as unresolved. There is no map to declare and none to align to.
Finding content is by address today, not by where the client is standing, so nothing declares an area a fabric or a server applies to and a client cannot test relevance by place.
